⚙️ Under the hood · Step 8 of 8 · 7 min

How a model picks the next token

Temperature, top-k and top-p, with the numbers in your hands.

🎲 The model gives a distribution, not a word

A language model does not output the next word directly. It gives a probability to every token in its vocabulary (all the tokens it can output): a probability distribution over the next token. Here is one for the prompt “The cat sat on the …”:

A decoding rule (also called a decoding strategy) turns the distribution into one token. The two simplest rules:
Greedy decoding: always take the most likely token. Here that is “mat”, every time.
Sampling: draw a token at random with these probabilities. The token “mat” comes up about half the time, “moon” about once in twenty draws.
Next tokenProbability
mat0.5
sofa0.2
floor0.15
roof0.1
moon0.05

The chosen token is added to the text, and everything repeats for the next position. A real vocabulary has tens of thousands of tokens or more; this toy one has five, to keep the sums short.

Task. Greedy decoding always takes the most likely token. What is its typical weakness in long texts?

Show the answer

Right answer: It gives repetitive text that can get stuck in a loop

Greedy decoding is deterministic: no random draw can break a repeating pattern. Once a phrase has appeared, the model can rate repeating it as even more likely, and then the same phrase comes back again and again. Sampling sometimes takes a less likely token, which keeps the text varied.

✂️ Top-k: keep the k best, then renormalise

Sampling from the whole distribution has the opposite weakness. A real distribution has a long tail of unlikely tokens. Each of them is rare, but together they can come up quite often, and one strange token can send the rest of the text in the wrong direction.

Top-k sampling cuts the tail off: set a number k, keep the k most likely tokens and drop the rest. Then divide each kept probability by their sum, so that they add up to 1 again: this is called renormalising. Only then draw a token.

k = 2: keep mat (0.5) and sofa (0.2)
their sum: 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7
sofa: 0.2 / 0.7 ≈ 0.29
mat: 0.5 / 0.7 ≈ ?

The tokens “floor”, “roof” and “moon” now have probability 0: they can no longer be drawn. You will work out the new probability of “mat” on the next screen.

Task. A language model's next-token probabilities are 0.5, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1 and 0.05. With top-k sampling and k = 2, what is the probability of the most likely token after renormalising, to two decimal places?

Show the solution

Top-k with k = 2 keeps only the two most likely tokens: 0.5 and 0.2. Their sum is 0.7, and dividing by it makes them add up to 1 again: 0.5 / 0.7 ≈ 0.71 and 0.2 / 0.7 ≈ 0.29. The other three tokens can no longer be drawn. With k = 1 only the top token would stay: greedy decoding again.

🧮 Top-p: keep the smallest set that reaches p

Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, does not fix the number of tokens. It fixes a share of the probability: a threshold p that you set, for example 0.9.

Sort the tokens from the most likely to the least likely and add up their probabilities one by one. Stop as soon as the sum reaches or passes p. Keep the tokens you have counted, drop the rest, renormalise and draw a token.

Next tokenProbabilitySum so far
mat0.50.5
sofa0.20.7
floor0.150.85
roof0.10.95
moon0.051

With p = 0.9 the sum first reaches the threshold at “roof” (0.95). So four tokens stay, and only “moon” is dropped. The kept set is called the nucleus.

Task. A language model's next-token probabilities, sorted from the largest, are 0.5, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1 and 0.05. With top-p (nucleus) sampling and p = 0.8, how many tokens stay as candidates?

Show the solution

0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7 is still below 0.8. Adding 0.15 gives 0.85, so the threshold is reached and 3 tokens stay. The token that takes the sum past p is kept too: the set has to cover at least p. The 3 kept probabilities are then renormalised: each is divided by 0.85.

Task. Top-k keeps the same number of tokens at every step. Why can top-p fit better?

Show the answer

Right answer: The number of tokens adapts: few when the model is sure, many when it is unsure

With p = 0.9, a top token at 0.95 stays alone, while five tokens at 0.2 each all stay: the set follows the shape of the distribution. A fixed k = 2 would add a weak token in the first case and throw away three good ones in the second. The two rules can also be used together.

🌡️ Temperature reshapes the distribution

Top-k and top-p cut the distribution. Temperature reshapes it. The model first computes a raw score for every token, its logit, and softmax turns the logits z into the probabilities p.

The temperature T is a positive number that you set: every logit is divided by T before softmax. T = 1 changes nothing.

T below 1 stretches the gaps between the logits: at T = 0.5 the logits (2, 1, 0) become (4, 2, 0). The distribution gets sharper, and the text more predictable. T above 1 shrinks the gaps: the distribution gets flatter, and the text more varied, with more strange tokens.

p = softmax(z / T)
p_i = e^(z_i / T) / Σ_j e^(z_j / T)
z = (2, 1, 0)
T = 1: p ≈ (0.67, 0.24, 0.09)
T = 0.5: p ≈ (0.87, 0.12, 0.02)
T = 2: p ≈ (0.51, 0.31, 0.19)

The order of the tokens never changes: at every T above 0 the largest logit keeps the largest probability. Only the gap between it and the others grows or shrinks.

Task. A language model samples the next token from softmax(z / T): z are its logits, T is the temperature. What happens as T goes down towards 0?

Show the answer

Right answer: Sampling comes close to greedy decoding: the top token takes almost everything

A tiny T makes the gaps between the logits huge, so softmax gives almost everything to the largest one: for the logits (2, 1, 0) and T = 0.1 the top token gets more than 0.9999. That is why many tools treat a temperature of 0 as greedy decoding. A very large T does the opposite: the distribution gets close to uniform.

Task. Two tokens have the logits (ln 3, 0). At T = 1 softmax gives them the probabilities (0.75, 0.25), because e^(ln 3) = 3 and e⁰ = 1. What is the probability of the first token at T = 0.5?

Show the solution

The logits become (2·ln 3, 0), and e^(2·ln 3) = 3² = 9, so the first probability is 9 / (9 + 1) = 0.9. Halving T squares the ratio of the two probabilities: from 3 : 1 to 9 : 1. At T = 2 the ratio would shrink to √3 : 1, and the first probability to about 0.63.

Task. You lower the temperature of a language model from 1 to 0.2. What does that do to its answers?

Show the answer

Right answer: They get more predictable, but a likely answer can still be false

A low temperature keeps the model close to its most likely continuations, so the answers vary less from run to run. But likely is not the same as true: if the top continuation is a mistake, a low temperature repeats that mistake reliably. Nothing in sampling checks the facts.

Remember

  • A language model outputs a probability distribution over the next token. A decoding rule picks one token: greedy decoding takes the top one, sampling draws at random.
  • Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to p or more, so the number of tokens follows the distribution. Both renormalise before sampling.
  • Temperature: softmax(z / T). T below 1 sharpens the distribution, T above 1 flattens it, and T → 0 gives greedy decoding.
  • Predictable is not the same as true: a low temperature does not check the facts.
